the two forms of CAH differ in their serological and HLA characteristics and that these differences are reflected in the cytoskeletal immunofluorescent reactivity.

there are two types of chronic hepatitis (CH) in the population studied, the HBV-associated and the autoimmune, that these types can be distinguished by their serological markers (HBsAg and anti-actin) and by their HLA profile, and that these differences are reflected by differences in the pattern of immunofluuorescence reactivity against cytoskeletal components.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the cellular and molecular basis of autoimmunity, and its application in the study of chronic hepatitis.
the immunogenetics of CAH, and with the role of cytoskeletal components in the pathogenesis of CAH, with the aim of understanding the pathogenesis of autoimmune diseases.
the immunopathogenesis of chronic liver disease, with the aim of defining the mechanisms by which liver injury is induced and perpetuated, in order to develop rational approaches to treatment.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the two types of CAH, the HBV-associated and autoimmune types, are distinguishable by the serological markers, and that these markers are related to the cytoskeletal components of the liver cells.

the autoimmune type of CAH, with antibody to cytoskeletal proteins, is associated with HLA B8 and DR3, while the HBV-associated form is associated with HLBW35 and DR2, with the former type more frequent in Australia and the latter more frequent in Yugoslavia.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the differences in the expression of CAH among populations are reflected by the patterns of immunoflurescence reactivity to components of the cytoskeleton, and that this is determined in part by the genetic and environmental influences which specify the HBV and autoimmune types.
the cytoskeletal reactivities, AC and IF, are useful markers for the autoimmune and viral forms of chronic liver disease.
